Across Europe, homes in cities cost far more than in the countryside. However, smaller gaps do not mean that homes are affordable. Euronews Business looks at where the gap is widest and why.

House prices in urban centres are, on average, 31% above the national average across 16 European countries, according to Euronews Business calculations based on the OECD’s Regions and Cities at a Glance 2026 report.

Prices are 11% below the national average in commuting zones and 30% below it in areas beyond cities and their commuting zones.

This is partly explained by the fact that jobs, investment and innovation are increasingly concentrated in capital regions and large cities. And people follow jobs and opportunities, the OECD says.

But the size of the gap between cities and the countryside varies widely across Europe.

Denmark, Hungary and Finland have the biggest gaps

In Denmark, house prices in urban centres are 64% above the national average, while prices outside cities are 51% below it. This is the largest gap among the European countries in the data.

This means homes cost about 3.4 times as much per square metre in urban centres as they do outside cities and their commuting zones.

Put another way, with the national average set at 100, prices stand at 164 in urban centres and 49 outside cities and their commuting zones.

Hungary follows, with city prices 57% above the national average and prices outside cities 45% below. In Finland, the figures are 55% above and 44% below.

Sweden (46% above and 42% below), Ireland (43% above and 36% below) and Portugal (38% above and 35% below) also show large gaps.

For Sweden and the other Nordic countries, Gabriel M. Ahlfeldt, a professor at Humboldt University in Berlin, pointed to “the contrast between strong demand in a limited number of urban labour markets and much weaker demand in sparsely populated areas.”

In Hungary, investment partly drives the gap, according to József Hegedüs, senior housing policy researcher at the Metropolitan Research Institute in Budapest. “A large part of the Budapest boom is speculative demand,” he told Euronews Business.

Smallest gaps in the Netherlands and the UK

The Netherlands and the UK record the smallest gaps among countries with data for both areas. In the Netherlands, city prices are just 1% above the national average and prices outside cities are 9% below. In the UK, city prices are 4% above the national average, while prices outside cities are also 9% below.

In every country in the European comparison except the Netherlands, homes in commuting zones are also cheaper than homes in urban centres.

Why are city homes more expensive?

“Cities concentrate jobs, universities, services and cultural amenities,” Ahlfeldt from Humboldt University told Euronews Business.

“Firms benefit from access to workers, customers and other firms, while households value both employment opportunities and urban life. This creates strong demand for well-connected locations.”

He said that demand translates into higher prices when construction is constrained by geography, planning rules or local opposition.

Why does the gap differ so much?

City prices range from 3.4 times those outside cities and their commuting zones in Denmark to 1.1 times in the Netherlands.

“The gap depends on how concentrated economic opportunities are, how well other places connect to them, and how readily housing supply responds,” Ahlfeldt said.

A country with one dominant employment centre and weak demand elsewhere can have a large price gap, he said. In a densely settled country, smaller towns and rural areas may offer good access to several employment centres, spreading housing demand more widely.

A small gap does not mean homes are affordable

“A small city–rural gap can coexist with severe affordability problems,” Ahlfeldt said.

In well-connected countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands, many towns and rural areas are within easy reach of major job centres, he said. This can make them highly desirable places to live.

He said the national figure hides big regional differences in the UK. A rural area in the South East can attract strong demand, while a city elsewhere can be much cheaper.

The OECD’s UK comparison also uses the median price of a whole home, so larger homes outside urban centres can narrow the measured gap.

“A small average gap should therefore not be read as evidence that London is affordable, or that access to employment no longer matters,” he said.

Munich and Chemnitz: a 17-year income gap

House prices also vary widely between cities in the same country. The OECD compared house prices with disposable income in metropolitan regions.

Germany had the widest gap between its metropolitan regions among the countries in the comparison. Buying a home in Munich takes the equivalent of about 17 more years of disposable income than buying one in Chemnitz, according to the OECD.

Ahlfeldt said Germany’s size alone cannot explain the gap. Munich combines strong employment opportunities with an attractive living environment and sustained competition for housing. Chemnitz has a different economic and demographic history, including the legacy of restructuring and population loss after reunification.

In 11 of the 13 countries with data, house prices in the largest metropolitan region are higher relative to local incomes than the average across metropolitan regions in that country.

The Netherlands is an exception, where the largest metropolitan region is slightly below the average.

Who is most affected?

“The key distinction is between people who already own property in expensive locations and those trying to gain access,” Ahlfeldt said.

He noted that young people, first-time buyers and renters entering the market face higher costs without the benefit of rising property values. Lower-paid workers providing essential urban services can face particularly difficult choices between housing costs, living space and commuting time.

“Above all young people without family wealth. In Hungary access to ownership increasingly depends on help from parents, and parents in the regions can give little,” Hegedüs said.

In some European cities, rent can take up an entire salary, or even more. In 2025, average net salaries in Lisbon and Istanbul were not enough to cover the rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the city centre.

Study finds that parents' use of mobile phones outside working hours is linked to poorer speech development in preschool children; researchers also warn that overly dependent family relationships can undermine youngsters' autonomy.

Parents' use of mobile phones outside working hours is linked to poorer speech development in their children. That is the conclusion of a study by RISE-Health and the University of Aveiro (source in Portuguese), which looked at how family functioning and the use of digital devices affect the phonological development of preschool-age children.

On the day the Universal Children's Rights Day is celebrated, the scientific study warns that "parents' use of mobile phones outside working hours, the child's use of a tablet during the night and excessively close and interdependent relationships are associated with delayed speech in children".

"Parents play a very important role in the communication opportunities they provide every day. Talking, playing, singing and telling stories allow the child to hear and try out speech sounds in situations that have meaning. It is equally important to give the child time to respond and take the initiative," explains Maria Inês Gomes, a researcher at RISE-Health, quoted in a statement.

According to the study "Screen use and family functioning as predictors of phonological development in children", which involved 93 families with children aged between 3 and 5 who speak European Portuguese, "the impact does not depend only on the amount of exposure, but also on the type of content and the context of use, since parents' attention, diverted to digital devices, can reduce face-to-face interactions, which are essential for language development".

The researcher also stresses that these findings "also invite adults to reflect on their own digital habits and to provide moments of attention and availability for their children free from the interference of screens".

Alongside the use of mobile devices after working hours, excessive dependence between parents and children also emerges as being linked to phonological development.

According to RISE-Health specialists, "family relationships that are excessively closed and highly dependent can limit the child's autonomy and the diversity of linguistic contexts in which they take part, which are essential for practising and learning speech sounds".

"When adults often answer for the child or anticipate what the child intends to say, there may be less room for the child to take part, communicate and have the chance to develop autonomy, particularly in terms of phonological development," says Maria Inês Gomes.

According to the coordinator of the study, "developing accessible programmes to support parenting and digital literacy" in partnership with municipalities, academies and schools can help parents organise routines, choose appropriate digital content, supervise the use of devices and create moments for conversation and play.

New alliances, commitments and funding could help protect Pacific island nations, restore degraded peatlands and tackle global food waste.

As COP31 draws to a close, some of the familiar tensions that have shadowed the UN’s climate summits for years are dominating the headlines again.

With draft agreements on the table, oil- and gas-producing nations such as Saudi Arabia have sought to weaken calls for a faster transition away from fossil fuels.

Meanwhile, a coalition of more than 130 developing countries is demanding that wealthy nations cut their own emissions faster and commit more climate funding in grants rather than loans, so that developing nations don’t get saddled with debt.

The summit has made headlines for more than its political disputes, though. Host country Türkiye unveiled its ‘35 by 35’ pledge, which aims to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 23 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.

But there have been plenty of small victories on the sidelines, too, including efforts to protect coral reefs and funds to help Pacific island nations cope with rising seas.

Here are 23 ways that COP31 has given us reason for optimism.

Food, agriculture and health wins at COP31

23. Funding to curb food waste

The IKEA Foundation announced a €40 million, four-year initiative that aims to scale up proven solutions – such as improving cold storage and converting food waste into organic fertiliser or animal feed – to cut food loss, prevent supply-chain waste, divert food from landfills and redistribute surplus food.

22. An initiative tackling food and water insecurity

The FAO launched the Turquoise Nexus Initiative to help countries facing water shortages and food insecurity improve irrigation systems, prepare for droughts and develop more water-efficient crops.

21. Funding for climate change and health research

The European Commission, British medical research foundation the Wellcome Trust and public funders from five continents launched the first global alliance dedicated to funding research involving climate change and human health.

20. Protection for those hit by conflict

Germany’s International Climate Initiative announced grants of €7-15 million per project to address the links between climate change and conflict, such as competition over dwindling water supplies and agricultural land.

Clean energy and technology wins at COP31

19. Support for clean energy in Africa

Italy and the UNDP will commit €10 million to support clean energy projects in Africa, potentially including biogas in Kenyan schools and digital electricity networks in Uganda.

18. Accolades for sustainable buildings

Through the International Sustainable Buildings Competition, COP31 and the UNEP recognised nine projects delivering measurable emissions cuts, including a Bangladesh garment factory that cut operational emissions by 78 per cent and an Irish university building that cut its energy consumption by 40.5 per cent.

17. Access to energy-efficient cooling

Italy, Switzerland and several charitable organisations pledged more than €15 million to improve access to energy-efficient cooling and protect communities in regions such as in Southeast Asia, South Asia and the Horn of Africa from extreme heat.

16. Tackling climate misinformation

A UN-backed initiative launched recommendations for tackling climate misinformation generated by AI, as well as a charter that aims to prevent advertisers from funding climate disinformation.

Climate finance and adaptation wins at COP31

15. Funds for environmental protection

Four governments – Belgium, Denmark, Germany and South Korea – pledged more than €180 million to Global Environment Facility funds supporting environmental protection and climate adaptation.

14. Protecting Pacific island nations from rising seas

The Asian Development Bank spearheaded a programme that aims to raise about €1 billion to protect 14 Pacific island countries from rising seas and extreme weather. 

13. A boost for early warning systems

Canada announced up to €6.5 million for the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems initiative, which helps vulnerable countries prepare for extreme weather.

12. Cleaning up the Mediterranean

An EU-funded programme called Interreg NEXT MED officially launched 49 projects worth more than €120 million in 15 Mediterranean countries – including Italy, Spain, Egypt and Lebanon – that address issues such as water management, biodiversity, clean energy and waste reduction.

Oceans, nature and biodiversity wins at COP31

11. Celebrating Ghana’s emissions cuts

Ghana has received 6.57 million carbon credits for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation. Expected to be worth about €40 million, the credits were issued under the Architecture for REDD+ Transactions (ART) and its TREES standard. Ghana is the first African country to receive these credits.

10. Hope for degraded peatlands

A new initiative called the Peatland Breakthrough aims to restore 30 million hectares of degraded peatlands and raise about €90 billion for conservation and climate action.

9. A reef conservation fund

The UN-backed Global Fund for Coral Reefs announced more than €27 million for reef conservation projects in 22 developing countries, including Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Indonesia, the Philippines and Tanzania.

8. Green initiatives at sea

A coalition of 27 countries launched the Blue NDC Implementation Taskforce to help secure funding and technical support for projects, such as cleaner shipping, offshore renewable energy and marine conservation. The EU also joined the Blue NDC Challenge, an initiative led by France and Brazil to help countries put the ocean commitments in their climate plans into practice.

7. Millions for coastal protection

Canada granted the Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance about €9 million in funding commitments from now through 2030 to finance projects that protect oceans and coastal communities from climate change.

6. Funding for local environmental initiatives

Germany opened a new funding round offering grants of €60,000-€200,000 for local organisations in developing nations that are working to cut emissions, protect biodiversityand help communities adapt to climate change.

5. Support for small-scale fishers

The European Commission unveiled its ‘From Water to Market’initiative to support small-scale fisheries, coastal livelihoods and food security across the Mediterranean.

4. Biodiversity action

Norway announced about €4.5 million in funding to help developing nations implement their national biodiversity action plans.

Climate pledges and accountability wins at COP 31

3. Paris Agreement’s second Global Stocktake

Despite tense talks throughout the conference, signatories of the Paris Agreement kicked off the second Global Stocktake, a two-year assessment of global progress towards meeting the agreement’s climate goals.

2. Methane leak monitoring

The UNEP revealed that its satellite-based monitoring system has helped stop five major methane leaks in Canada, Iraq, Kazakhstan and Mexico since June, preventing an estimated 125,000 tonnes of methane from reaching the atmosphere. So far, though, just nine of the 159 countriesbehind the Global Methane Pledge have endorsed a new declaration reaffirming their goal of cutting global methane emissions by at least 30 per cent from 2020 levels by 2030.

1. Fossil fuel phaseouts

During COP31, Finland affirmed its commitment to TAFF by publishing a national roadmap, following in the footsteps of France, Germany and the Netherlands. Denmark, Portugal, Luxembourg and Spain later announced their own national plans.

Hungary is set to lift its objections to Ukraine’s last two EU accession clusters on Friday, diplomats say, allowing Kyiv and Moldova to start negotiating on every aspect of EU membership.

Hungary is set to drop its veto on opening Ukraine’s final two EU accession negotiating clusters at a meeting of EU ambassadors on Friday, two diplomatic sources have told Euronews.

András Bíró-Nagy, Hungary’s Secretary of State for EU Affairs at the Prime Minister’s Office, signalled the move during a discussion on enlargement ahead of Thursday’s General Affairs Council in Brussels.

Budapest has long held up Ukraine’s accession bid by blocking the opening of negotiating clusters. Its veto has also stalled Moldova’s membership bid, which remains linked to Kyiv’s.

Hungary’s position began to shift after Péter Magyar ousted Viktor Orbán following 16 years in power. The first negotiating cluster was opened in June, a second in July and two more in October.

Last month, Kyiv and Budapest reached an agreement on the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine, which the Ukrainian parliament subsequently passed.

The Hungarian government was then ready to move forward but held off for several more weeks on opening the final two clusters. Years of anti-Ukrainian rhetoric under Orbán had made the move politically difficult at home.

Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held their first bilateral meeting on the margins of the last European Council summit in Brussels on 16 October, marking another step in the warming of the relations between the two neighbours.

Once Hungary confirms on Friday that it is lifting the veto, Ukraine and Moldova are due to open all negotiating clusters, including some of the most sensitive chapters, on the environment and agriculture.

Agriculture will be particularly sensitive for Kyiv. The European Commission has proposed to carve out access to EU funding and the European market for certain Ukrainian agricultural products, under pressure from countries such as Poland and France.

Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi told Euronews Kyiv could not accept a permanent exclusion of its farmers from the European market, but that the measures had to be transitional and proportionate.

Opening the clusters is only the beginning. Candidates must then align with EU legislation and practice, and throughout the process, member states can veto progress more than 100 times.

Gold and silver also fell as the dollar held near a 19-month high and investors bet on a US interest rate rise in December. South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 both fell 4.5% in morning trading. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 dropped 1.6%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell nearly 2%, and the Shanghai Composite lost 1.7%. AI-powered tools are offering new ways to help people with Alzheimer’s reconnect with personal memories.

Watching someone you love gradually lose their memories can be a painful experience. For Hilde Vautmans, that meant seeing her father eventually stop recognising her.

“That is something that hurts so much you cannot even describe it,” said Vautmans, a Belgian member of the European Parliament.

Like Vautmans, many people across Europe watch family members with dementia struggle to recall personal stories and shared experiences.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia and is associated with progressive cognitive decline, including difficulties with memory, thinking and communication. Dementia currently affects over 12 million people in Europe, with numbers projected to increase to 20 million by 2050. Alzheimer’s accounts for 60% to 80% of cases. 

Researchers say earlier diagnosis could help funnel people into treatment while the disease is still mild. Others are trying to improve the lives of people already experiencing memory loss, for example through reminiscence therapy. Traditionally, this approach involves using familiar objects, photographs and music to prompt people to recall and share experiences from their lives.

Now, proponents of reminiscence therapy are eyeing virtual reality, interactive platforms, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technological tools to create more personalised experiences and help people reconnect with their memories.

One of these initiatives is Synthetic Memories, a project from the Barcelona-based creative studio Domestic Data Streamers. It uses AI to recreate people’s memories and turn them into images, offering a new approach to preserving personal stories.

The project's work with people living with dementia began in 2023 in care homes for older people, including residents with Alzheimer’s and other forms of dementia. The studio worked with social workers and neurotherapists in Spain for the project.

During a one-hour session with someone suffering memory loss, an interviewer and an AI prompter guide participants through their memories. Generative AI models are then used to create visual representations of the experiences they describe.

The project stresses that it is not intended as a cure, but as a tool to support reminiscence therapy.

Synthetic Memories has since hit the road as part of The Memory Radio Station, a travelling exhibition launched in partnership with pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly. It is touring Europe to bring conversations about memory loss into public spaces.

The exhibition invites members of the public to share their own memories, transforming spoken and written stories into AI images. They do not need to be suffering from memory loss to participate.

In November, the exhibition is at the European Parliament in Brussels. That’s where Vautmans took part, recalling childhood memories and time spent with her father.

She recalled going with him to the cow market in Sint-Truiden, the Belgian town where she grew up.

“Those were wonderful moments with my father when I could go with him to the market and try to sell the cows and then put them on the scale [to weigh them]”, she told the radio station.

Recognising the symptoms and obtaining an early diagnosis are also crucial to improving quality of life for people with Alzheimer’s.

“In our case, it took a long time. It was a whole search; it was a denial,” Vautmans told Euronews. “It’s not Alzheimer’s; it’s just stress, it’s just too much work. Like we all say when we see somebody forgetting things”.

Why early diagnosis matters

Evidence shows that people who receive an early and accurate diagnosis experience improved psychosocial outcomes, including reduced anxiety and greater independence, the Alzheimer’s Society noted in its latest report.

An early diagnosis also allows people to access treatments and interventions that address their clinical and care needs, with some treatments being most effective in the earlier stages of the disease.

Yet one of the main barriers to an early Alzheimer’s diagnosis is limited awareness of the disease and its symptoms.

A recent Europe-wide survey found significant gaps in public knowledge about dementia. Among 681 people surveyed in 12 countries, fewer than half knew that Alzheimer's disease is the most common type of dementia, while many people said Alzheimer’s cannot be prevented and is simply a normal part of ageing.

While there is no guaranteed way to prevent Alzheimer’s, lifestyle factors such as diet, exercise and smoking can affect someone’s risk.

“Without adequate knowledge, it can be difficult to spot the signs of different dementia subtypes,” the authors wrote. They said raising awareness among the general public could help people recognise symptoms and seek a diagnosis sooner.

That’s where the travelling exhibition comes in. It aims to encourage people to reflect on the importance of memory and the impact of Alzheimer’s disease.

“This is an engagement opportunity that demonstrates what is making us unique as human beings; that's the power of our brain,” Frederic Destrebecq, executive director of the European Brain Council, said at the opening of the exhibition in Brussels.

“This is a reminder of how essential it is to look after and protect our best asset in life.”

The Trump administration pressed ahead with the auction despite a federal judge’s finding that regulators broke wildlife protection law and conservation groups vowed to have the leases voided.

The Trump administration on Thursday sold the first deep-sea mining leases in US history, offering seabed areas off American Samoa just days after a federal court found the approval process unlawful.

The sale covered two zones totalling about 31 million acres (12.5 million hectares) in the Pacific, in the face of strong opposition from local residents and environmental groups.

Each zone fetched $3 million (about €2.8 million), for a combined $6 million (about €5.5 million). The winning bidders have not been named.

On Monday, a federal judge in Hawaii sided with community and conservation groups, finding that the National Marine Fisheries Service broke the Endangered Species Act when it cleared the sale.

But despite the court's ruling, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum called it “the first time the United States has held an offshore critical minerals lease sale in the Pacific and a historic step for America’s energy and mineral security.”

He said the sale “opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”

Mining firms want to harvest polymetallic nodules from the deep ocean floor. The potato-sized lumps contain nickel, copper and cobalt, metals used in batteries and electric vehicle systems.

The sale follows an executive order Trump signed in April 2025 describing leadership in deep-sea science and technology as “a core national security and economic interest.”

It also answers a request from the US company Impossible Metals to open leasing off the territory, which lies east of the independent nation of Samoa.

Opposition from locals and scientists

Critics warn of damage that could not be undone, with clouds of waste smothering marine life and noise from heavy machinery disrupting animal migrations.

“This premature push to exploit the deep sea before we even fully understand how vital it is will have catastrophic consequences that reverberate for generations,” said Julia Singer, Oceana’s Defense Campaign Manager.

American Samoa banned deep-sea mining in its own territorial waters in 2024, but the auction covers the federally controlled Outer Continental Shelf beyond that limit.

In a public comment in September, Governor Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula said he “does not support commercial deep-sea mineral extraction at this time.”

In Monday's ruling, Judge Jill Otake wrote, “NMFS failed to even attempt to consider the potential effects on ESA-listed species”

The lease areas lie close to the vast Rose Atoll marine sanctuary, home to many endangered or threatened species, including whales, turtles, sharks and corals.

Earthjustice attorney Chris Eaton condemned the decision to go ahead.

“In deciding to move forward with today’s scheduled sale, the Trump administration has performed a renegade, unlawful act,” he said. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided.”
